title: Gudinas v. State
description: Whether Thomas Lee Gudinas's claims for postconviction relief and public records should be granted, with Gudinas arguing that his mental state and age at the time of the crime, along with constitutional challenges to state procedures and clemency record confidentiality, warrant relief, and the State arguing that these claims are procedurally barred and meritless.
plaintiff_argument: Gudinas argues that his lifelong mental illnesses and brain impairment, along with his age of twenty at the time of the crime, should exempt him from execution under an extension of Atkins and Roper. He also contends that Florida's Eighth Amendment conformity clause and the application of procedural bar rule 3.851(d)(2) are unconstitutional, and he is entitled to public records related to the clemency process.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Gudinas's claims are untimely, procedurally barred because they could have been raised in prior proceedings, lack merit as existing precedent does not support extending Atkins or Roper to his circumstances, and that clemency records are confidential and exempt from public disclosure.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's orders summarily denying Gudinas's third successive motion for postconviction relief and denying his demand for public records, and also denied his motion for a stay of execution.

title: Bojorquez v. State
description: Whether the 2017 repeal of a law that declared taxicab certificates and permits as "private property" implicates the Florida Constitution's Takings Clause, requiring compensation.
plaintiff_argument: The taxicab companies argued that the 2017 repeal constituted a taking of their "private property" (PTC-issued certificates and permits) without compensation, in violation of the Florida Constitution's Takings Clause.
defendant_argument: The State and Hillsborough County argued that no taking occurred because the PTC-issued certificates and permits were not "private property" for Takings Clause purposes, but rather revocable privileges or licenses.
decision_outcome: The court held that the 2017 repeal does not implicate the Florida Constitution's Takings Clause, affirming that the PTC-issued certificates and permits were not irrevocable private property.

title: Jackson v. Florida
description: Whether the 2023 amendments to Florida's capital sentencing statute, allowing a non-unanimous jury recommendation for death, are constitutional and were properly applied to Michael James Jackson's resentencing.
plaintiff_argument: Jackson argued that the 2023 amendments, which permit a death sentence recommendation with eight or more jurors, are unconstitutional, violate his Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment rights (arbitrariness, racial discrimination, equal protection), Sixth Amendment right to unanimity, constitute a bill of attainder, were retroactively applied, and that the jury instructions were misleading. He also claimed errors in excluding mitigating evidence, precluding witness impeachment, and prosecutorial misconduct.
defendant_argument: The State of Florida argued that the 2023 amendments are constitutional and were properly applied prospectively to Jackson's resentencing. They contended that the Eighth Amendment does not require a unanimous jury recommendation for death, that there was no racially discriminatory intent, and that the procedural changes were correctly applied. They also asserted that the court's instructions were not misleading, a codefendant's sentence is not mitigating, and no prosecutorial misconduct or other errors warrant a new penalty phase.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the death sentences imposed at Jackson's resentencing, rejecting all of his challenges to the 2023 amendments and the resentencing proceedings.

title: Black Voters Matter v. Byrd
description: Whether Florida's 2022 congressional districting plan violates the state's Non-Diminishment Clause by reducing Black voters' ability to elect representatives, or if the previous district was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander under the Equal Protection Clause.
plaintiff_argument: The Enacted Plan violates the Florida Constitution's Non-Diminishment Clause by eliminating a district where Black voters could elect their preferred candidates, and that complying with the Non-Diminishment Clause is a compelling state interest.
defendant_argument: The Enacted Plan is valid because the previous district (Benchmark CD 5) would constitute an unconstitutional racial gerrymander under the Equal Protection Clause, and the Legislature's obligation to comply with the Equal Protection Clause is superior to the Non-Diminishment Clause.
decision_outcome: The court upheld Florida's 2022 congressional districting plan, finding that the federal Equal Protection Clause prohibits the racially gerrymandered district that the plaintiffs sought to retain.

title: State v. Penna
description: Whether a defendant's Fifth Amendment Miranda rights are automatically violated when an officer fails to re-read a Miranda warning following a defendant's voluntary re-initiation of contact, with the plaintiff arguing it is not automatically violated and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the previous state precedent (Shelly) requiring a categorical re-warning of Miranda rights after a defendant voluntarily re-initiates contact is inconsistent with U.S. Supreme Court precedent and should be receded from.
defendant_argument: Penna argued that his statements were obtained in violation of Miranda because the officer failed to re-read his Miranda rights prior to custodial interrogation, as required by state precedent (Shelly and Quarles).
decision_outcome: The court answered the certified question in the negative, ruling that Miranda rights are not automatically violated when an officer fails to re-read warnings after a defendant voluntarily re-initiates contact, and receded from its prior decision in Shelly.

title: Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re: Adult Personal Use of Marijuana
description: Whether the proposed amendment to legalize adult personal use of marijuana in Florida satisfies constitutional and statutory requirements for placement on the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed amendment complies with the single-subject rule, the ballot summary is clear, and it is not facially invalid under the federal constitution.
defendant_argument: The proposed amendment violates the single-subject rule, the ballot summary is misleading and lacks clarity, and it is preempted by federal law, making it facially invalid.
decision_outcome: The court approved the proposed amendment for placement on the ballot.

title: Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re: Limiting Government Interference with Abortion
description: Whether a proposed citizen initiative amendment to the Florida Constitution, titled "Amendment to Limit Government Interference with Abortion," is valid for placement on the ballot, considering single-subject requirements, ballot clarity, and facial validity under the U.S. Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General and other opponents argued that the proposed amendment violates the single-subject rule, that the ballot title and summary are misleading by omission of material legal effects, and that it is facially invalid under the U.S. Constitution due to preemption by federal law.
defendant_argument: The Sponsor and other proponents argued that the proposed amendment addresses a single subject, that the ballot title and summary are clear and accurately reflect the chief purpose, and that it is not facially invalid under the U.S. Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court approved the proposed amendment for placement on the ballot, finding it complies with single-subject requirements, ballot title and summary clarity, and is not facially invalid under the U.S. Constitution.

title: Worrell v. Desantis
description: Whether Governor Ron DeSantis properly suspended State Attorney Monique H. Worrell for neglect of duty and incompetence, or if the suspension order was impermissibly vague and infringed upon her prosecutorial discretion.
plaintiff_argument: Worrell argued that the allegations in the Executive Order were impermissibly vague and addressed conduct that fell within the lawful exercise of prosecutorial discretion, thus challenging the Governor's suspension power.
defendant_argument: Governor DeSantis argued that Worrell's practices constituted neglect of duty and incompetence by allowing violent offenders, drug traffickers, serious juvenile offenders, and pedophiles to evade incarceration, and by preventing assistant state attorneys from obtaining mandatory minimum sentences and enhancements, thereby justifying her suspension under the Florida Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Court denied Worrell's petition for a writ of quo warranto, upholding the Governor's suspension from office.

title: Planned Parenthood v. Florida
description: Whether the recently amended Florida statute prohibiting abortions after 15 weeks of gestation conflicts with the Florida Constitution's Privacy Clause.
plaintiff_argument: The statute violates the Privacy Clause of the Florida Constitution, which guarantees a right to abortion.
defendant_argument: The Privacy Clause does not encompass a right to abortion, and therefore the statute is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Florida Constitution's Privacy Clause does not provide a basis to invalidate the 15-week abortion ban, denying the temporary injunction sought by Planned Parenthood.

title: Tallahassee v. Florida Police Benevolent Association
description: Whether Marsy's Law grants a categorical right to anonymity for victims, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Florida Police Benevolent Association (FPBA) argued that police officers, as victims of assault, are entitled to Marsy's Law protections, including the right to prevent the disclosure of their personal identifying information, such as their names.
defendant_argument: The City of Tallahassee and the News Media Coalition argued that Marsy's Law does not grant a categorical right for victims to remain anonymous, and therefore, the names of the police officers should be released.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Marsy's Law does not preclude the City from releasing the names of the two police officers, quashing the First District Court of Appeal's decision.

title: Boan v. Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal Judicial Nominating Commission
description: Whether judicial nominating commissions can nominate candidates who do not reside in the territorial jurisdiction of the applicable court at the time of nomination, and whether alleged violations of commission procedural rules are subject to quo warranto proceedings.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argue that the Florida Constitution and the commissions' own rules of procedure require judicial nominees to reside in the territorial jurisdiction of the court at the time of nomination, and that the commissions exceeded their authority by nominating non-resident candidates.
defendant_argument: The respondents argue that the constitutional residency requirement for judges attaches at the time of appointment, not nomination, and that the commissions did not exceed their constitutional authority. They also contend that alleged noncompliance with procedural rules is not a proper subject for a quo warranto proceeding.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitions, ruling that the constitutional residency requirement for judges attaches at the time of appointment, not nomination, and that alleged noncompliance with procedural rules is not a proper subject for a quo warranto proceeding.

title: Statler v. State
description: Whether Florida's sexual battery statute, section 794.011(5)(b), is facially unconstitutional or must be read to include a requirement that the State prove a criminal defendant knew or should have known the victim did not consent to sexual intercourse.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Garrett Statler, argued that the sexual battery statute is unconstitutional unless it requires the State to prove the defendant knew or should have known the victim did not consent, to satisfy due process.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Florida, argued that the statute is constitutional as written, requiring proof of the victim's non-consent but not the defendant's knowledge of that non-consent, as it is a general intent crime.
decision_outcome: The court found the sexual battery statute constitutional and affirmed the district court's decision upholding Statler's conviction.

title: Thourtman v. Junior
description: Whether Article I, section 14 of the Florida Constitution prohibits a trial court from detaining a defendant beyond first appearance without setting reasonable conditions for pretrial release unless the court has made a preliminary finding that the proof of guilt is evident or the presumption is great.
plaintiff_argument: Thourtman argued that Article I, section 14 requires a preliminary finding at first appearance that the proof of guilt is evident or the presumption is great before a defendant can be detained beyond first appearance without pretrial release.
defendant_argument: The State argued that a trial court may defer ruling on pretrial release and detain a defendant for a reasonable time to conduct a 'full' Arthur hearing, even without a preliminary finding of 'proof evident, presumption great' at first appearance.
decision_outcome: The court approved the Third District's holding, concluding that Article I, section 14 does not prohibit a trial court from detaining a defendant beyond first appearance without a preliminary finding of 'proof evident, presumption great' at first appearance.

title: In re Senate Joint Resolution of Legislative Apportionment 100
description: Whether the House and Senate apportionment plans in Senate Joint Resolution 100 are valid under the Florida Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General, House, and Senate argued that the apportionment plans comply with all constitutional standards, including population equality, compactness, boundary utilization, and protections against political favoritism and minority vote dilution.
defendant_argument: No party appeared to challenge the Legislature's apportionment plans, so there was no explicit defendant argument.
decision_outcome: The court declared the House and Senate apportionment plans in Senate Joint Resolution 100 to be valid.

title: State v. Dortch
description: Whether there is a "fundamental error" exception to the rule requiring a criminal defendant to file a motion to withdraw a plea in the trial court before appealing an involuntary plea, with the State arguing no such exception exists and Dortch arguing one should be recognized for due process.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Florida (Petitioner) argued that the Fourth District erred by allowing Dortch to directly appeal his convictions without first filing a motion to withdraw his plea, asserting there is no fundamental-error exception to the preservation requirement.
defendant_argument: Vernson Edward Dortch (Respondent) argued that a fundamental-error exception should apply, allowing him to appeal without first filing a motion to withdraw his plea, especially because the trial court's failure to hold a competency hearing violated his due process rights.
decision_outcome: The court held that there is no fundamental-error exception to the preservation requirement for appealing an involuntary plea, quashed the Fourth District's decision, and remanded with instructions to affirm Dortch's convictions and sentences.

title: Emerson v. Hillsborough County
description: Whether a Hillsborough County Charter amendment, adopted by voter initiative, is constitutionally valid when it imposes a transportation sales surtax and includes elaborate directives for allocating tax proceeds that conflict with state law granting the county commission authority to allocate such funds.
plaintiff_argument: The entire charter amendment, including the surtax, is unconstitutional because the spending directives are inseparable from the tax levy and conflict with state law, thus the trial court erred in severing them.
defendant_argument: The charter amendment is constitutional, or at least the surtax and valid portions should be upheld through severability, as its primary purpose (funding transportation) can still be achieved.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's judgment, ruling that the entire charter amendment, including the transportation sales surtax and its spending directives, is unconstitutional and cannot be severed.

title: Casiano v. State
description: Whether a defendant's potential designation as a prison releasee reoffender is a sufficient collateral legal consequence to prevent an appeal from being dismissed as moot after the sentence has been served, with the plaintiff arguing it is a sufficient consequence and the defendant arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: Casiano argued that his potential future designation as a prison releasee reoffender (PRR) under section 775.082(9)(a) 1. was a sufficient collateral legal consequence of his state prison sentence, precluding dismissal of his appeal as moot.
defendant_argument: The State, aligning with the Fourth District Court of Appeal, argued that Casiano's appeal was moot because he had completed his prison sentence, and his potential future designation as a prison releasee reoffender was not a sufficient collateral legal consequence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Florida approved the Fourth District's decision, holding that a defendant's potential designation as a prison releasee reoffender is not a sufficient collateral legal consequence to preclude dismissal of an appeal as moot when the sentence has been served.
